chapters.title: Cancellation curves
chapters.subtitle: why Euler's line of primes stops where it does

lines.text: Every composite number is a product: u times u plus d. Fix the gap d, let u run, and the products line up on one curve of the spiral. These are the cancellation curves.
Each curve is born at the number d plus one, the little ring, and everything after its birth is composite. A prime sits on exactly one curve: the one born at it.
Gap zero is the squares, gap one the pronic numbers. On the saddle every one of these curves climbs the ridge, because a product of two nearly equal numbers lands near the x axis.

Flatten the saddle and follow Euler's line, k squared plus k plus forty-one, past its forty primes. Wherever it meets a cancellation curve the value is composite, and the meetings come in two families.
Family one: at k equal to forty plus a square, the value is the product of two neighbouring values of the line itself. Forty-one times forty-three, forty-three times forty-seven, and on it goes.

Family two reaches in from a sister line, four j squared plus one hundred and sixty-three: a value of the sister times a value of Euler. Both families are products in one quadratic ring, the ring of root minus one sixty-three, and that is all the arithmetic there is.
Now ask the zeros instead. The master wave of all ten thousand zeros, evaluated along the line, spikes at every prime value and dips at every crossing. The zeros and the curves agree point by point.

chapters.title: Level contours
chapters.subtitle: slicing the saddle at a height

lines.text: The saddle is z equals x squared minus y squared, scaled down. Slice it with a horizontal plane and the cut is a hyperbola: opening left and right above the middle, up and down below it.

Here are the cuts at heights fifteen and thirty on the ridge side, opening along the squares and pronic rays. Every number lit on one contour shares the same value of n times the cosine of four pi root n.
Below the middle, on the valley side, the contours open along the y axis instead. The valley is where the one-to-four products live: u times four u plus an odd number.
Seen from the side the planes are real cuts through the surface. The valley planes also cut the trail of zeta rising from the centre: a plane at minus h meets the trail at the dial value four h.
At height zero the hyperbola collapses into the two diagonals, and a third family hugs them: the one-to-sixteen products. Each direction of the saddle collects its own family of products.

And the quantity shared along every contour, n cosine four pi root n, is the first harmonic of Voronoi's formula for the divisor function. The saddle is not decoration: its level lines are the contour lines of the divisor wave.

chapters.title: The bend as a probe
chapters.subtitle: a fixed plane sweeps the curves as the saddle bends

lines.text: Start flat. The ridge family in orange, the valley family in blue, the diagonal family in white, all drawn on a flat spiral. A plane at height fifteen touches nothing yet.
Bend the saddle a quarter of the way. The plane at minus fifteen now cuts the valley near the rim, around n equals thirteen hundred and seventy, and lights every number it crosses.
Half the bend, and the contour has moved inward to n near six hundred and eighty. The valley curves dive faster now, so the plane reads them off closer to the centre.
The tour's own bend, one. The contour sits at n three hundred and forty, and each blue curve crosses it in exactly one place: the plane is reading the curves like the teeth of a comb.

Bend it twice as hard and the contour closes in to n near one hundred and seventy. Nothing on the vertical planes has moved: the ridge still holds the squares and the pronics, the valley still holds the one-to-four products.
So the bend is a probe, not a parameter of the arithmetic. It decides which contour a plane picks, never which numbers sit on which curve. Sweeping it maps where every curve crosses that height.
Back to the tour's saddle. What the plane found on the way is the geometry of the curves themselves: where each family climbs, dives, or stays level.

chapters.title: Mirrors, not oracles
chapters.subtitle: the vortices of the chain at a zero

lines.text: This is the chain at the hundred and fifty-ninth zero: every link one term of the series, curling into vortices before it settles. Let's find their eyes with nothing but the turning angles.
Where the turn between links flips through a half-turn, the chain folds back on itself. That knot is an eye. Where the turn flips through zero the chain runs straight: a spoke, the edge of a vortex.

A vortex drawn by dozens of links is certain; one drawn by two or three is a guess, so its ring is faded. Now the crosses: the chain's own first vertices, reflected and turned by twice the Gram phase.
They land inside the rings. At the thousandth zero, with far more links, every eye out to the twelfth sits on its mirror to a thousandth. The far end of the chain is its near end in a mirror.
Stack the zeros as planes and trace each eye through them. Vortex one, in cyan, winds once around the axis per zero on a circle of radius exactly one. Vortex two rides an epicycle on it.
Take the Gram phase out and the whole tower collapses: vortex one to a single point, vortex two to a circle, vortex three to an epicycle. These are the chain's first terms, nothing more.
All ten thousand zeros seen down the axis: the unit circle of vortex one, the rings of the rest. This is as much structure as there is.

With the phase removed: the point, the circle, the epicycles. The eye angle at a zero reads that zero's Gram offset. It correlates with the next gap at minus a quarter, and with the next zero's offset not at all.
So each vortex is a mirror of the zero it sits at: the chain's own beginning, reflected through that zero's phase. It is not an oracle for the zero to come. Mirrors, not oracles.

chapters.title: Two counting problems
chapters.subtitle: the saddle and its half-twist

lines.text: Count the whole-number points under the curve u times v equals x. Each one is a factor pair, a point on a cancellation curve. The count grows like x log x, and the white line is how it wobbles around that. Each faint line marks one turn of the spiral.
Voronoi wrote that wobble as a sum of waves, one cosine of four pi root n x for each n. Here they arrive one by one, and the cyan sum settles onto the white.
The first wave on its own goes up and down twice on every turn of the spiral. That is the saddle itself. The surface the tour is drawn on is the first wave of the divisor problem.
Now count the points inside a circle of radius root x instead. There are about pi x of them, and this count wobbles too.
Hardy found its waves: two pi root n x, weighted by the number of ways to write n as a sum of two squares. They run half as fast, one up and down per turn. Watch them add up.

A wave that rises once per turn needs a different surface. Twist the saddle by half a turn for every turn of the spiral. The squares slide onto the crests and fall away, the pronic numbers slide into the troughs and rise, and the orange wave slows from two crests per turn to one.

So the two counting problems have two surfaces. The divisor wobble, made of the points on the cancellation curves, rides on two waves per turn: the saddle. The circle wobble, made of the points on the mirror lines, rides on one wave per turn: the saddle's half-twist.
Both wobbles are believed to grow no faster than about the fourth root of x. For neither problem has anyone proved it.

chapters.title: Primes of Euler's ring
chapters.subtitle: a second set of zeros

lines.text: Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one measures the size of numbers in a ring built on the square root of minus one hundred sixty-three. In that ring some ordinary primes break into two pieces. They split. The others stay whole.

Only a prime that splits can divide one of Euler's numbers, and the first prime that splits is forty-one. That is why his first forty values are all prime. Gold marks the primes that split, blue the primes that stay whole.

The zeros of zeta build a wave that rises at every prime, by the explicit formula. Here they arrive, all five and a half thousand below height six thousand. Every prime gets the same needle, every prime square half of one.

Now a second set of zeros: the zeros of the L-function of minus one sixty-three, ten thousand four hundred and sixty-two of them below the same height, computed for this. As they join, the needles at the blue primes sink away and the gold ones double.
Below forty-one nothing is left standing except four, nine, sixteen and twenty-five: squares of primes that stay whole, which are the sizes of those primes inside the ring.
Together the two sets of zeros count the primes of Euler's ring. Every composite value of his polynomial, every crossing of a cancellation curve with his line, is built from the gold spikes.
The extra zeros say which primes can divide Euler's numbers, which is what one Legendre symbol already says. They do not say which of his values are prime.

chapters.title: Mirror lines
chapters.subtitle: one pair proves a prime, two pairs factor

lines.text: On the squares side of the spiral the cancellation curves are k squared minus m squared. Every value is a difference of two squares, so every value factors.
Reflect them across the squares ray and the minus becomes a plus. They swing over into k squared plus m squared: sums of two squares.
Through every number pass some pairs of these mirror lines, one pair for each way to write it as a sum of two squares. Gold numbers have exactly one pair. Red numbers have two or more.
One pair proves a prime. Sixteen oh one is forty squared plus one squared, and no other pair of squares. So it is prime. This is Euler's criterion.

Two pairs prove a composite, and hand over a factor. Two twenty-one is fourteen squared plus five squared and also eleven squared plus ten squared. One greatest common divisor turns those into seventeen.
Eleven oh five sits on four pairs, and its factors fall out the same way: thirteen, five and seventeen.

Fermat works the other side of the mirror. He walks out along the squares until m squared minus n is itself a square. For fifteen oh one that takes ten steps, and the curve he finds is the cancellation curve through it.
Euler's test works only for his sixty-five idoneal numbers, and both methods are slower than modern tests. What the spiral adds is the picture: one search on each side of the mirror.

chapters.title: The discriminant comb
chapters.subtitle: one quadratic per plane

lines.text: Every curve on the spiral is a quadratic. Far from the centre it straightens into a line, and its distance from its ray is set by one number, its discriminant.
Slide a vertical plane across the squares side and it picks up one quadratic at a time. Red when the quadratic factors. Blue or green when it does not.
Count the primes on every plane, for k up to three thousand. Only the planes whose quadratic factors come up empty.
The white ticks are the Hardy–Littlewood predictions, from the discriminant alone. They match the counts with a correlation of 0.9995.

On the pronic side, Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one is the record, at discriminant minus one sixty-three. And a line among the cancellation curves, k squared plus k minus one, beats Landau's k squared plus one.

Two of these curves meet only where the difference of their discriminants factors. Euler's line and k squared plus one meet at exactly two numbers, one ninety-seven and sixteen oh one, and both are prime.

chapters.title: Pinching the spiral
chapters.subtitle: four ways to pile up the primes

lines.text: A pinch brings far-apart parts of the spiral together, so whatever they share piles up in one place. First, the fold: double every angle, and the squares ray and the pronic ray fall onto one ray.
Now every quadratic straightens at a distance set by its discriminant alone, from both sides at once. The two half combs merge into one comb of every discriminant.

The prime two shows up as a stripe. Lines whose discriminant is five mod eight never take an even value, and they average four hundred and thirty-eight primes. The lines at one mod eight are always even.
The residue pinch slides every number around its own circle to the angle two pi n over m. The spiral collapses onto m arms, one for each remainder.

The primes ride only the arms that share no factor with m. Modulo thirty that is eight arms, each almost four times richer in primes. The rest are cancellation arms, and their only prime is the one dividing thirty.
Pinched modulo four on the saddle, the two prime arms are exactly its two rising lobes, and the even numbers fall away down the valleys.
The pleat folds each turn into thirty slots after the pronic ray, and slot j becomes the curve k squared plus k plus j.

The primes gather on two curves named by Euler's lucky numbers, k squared plus k plus eleven, and plus seventeen. The white marks are the composites the pleat cannot see, built from primes larger than five.
On the squares side a curve takes both odd and even values, so it can never dodge two. That is why the prime-rich Euler lines all live on the pronic side.
Pinch by three, five and seven at once, as three axes, and every odd number falls into one cell of a lattice. The primes fill exactly the forty-eight cells off the three zero planes.

Every pinch gathers primes the way the sieve does, and no better: the best curve is richer by the product of p over p minus one, for the primes it sees. Euler's line sees every prime up to thirty-seven. The pinch shows the sieve as geometry. It cannot beat it.

chapters.title: The 12 × 12 torus
chapters.subtitle: turn and step, counted in twelves

lines.text: Every number on the spiral has two coordinates. Its turn is the ring it sits on, and its step is how far round that ring it has come from the square that starts it. Forty-one is six squared plus five: turn six, step five.
Count turn and step in twelves, and every number lands on a twelve by twelve board. Here come the primes up to ten million, each dropped into its cell.

Above three, the primes land in only forty-eight of the hundred and forty-four cells: the cells where the number leaves remainder one, five, seven or eleven after division by twelve. Two and three are the only primes anywhere else.
On this board every curve of the spiral becomes a straight line. The curves k squared plus k plus c run diagonally. Follow c equal to five and eleven: every cell they cross is gold.
One and seven cross gold in eight rows out of twelve. Three and nine, in four. Even values of c never cross gold at all, so those lines carry no primes.

On average, a line's share of the primes is three times its share of gold rows: three for five and eleven, two for one and seven, one for three and nine, nothing for the rest. Euler's forty-one, seventeen and eleven all sit in the top class.

The vertical lines are the curves on the other side of the spiral, k squared plus C. None of them stays gold for more than half its rows, so none can beat one and a half. That is why the prime-rich lines all live on the pronic side.
Roll the board up, the step the short way round and the turn the long way, and it becomes a torus. The two gold diagonals close into loops that wind once around it both ways.
Back on the spiral, the gold lines are Euler's family. Everything the board shows comes from dividing by two and three. It cannot see a single prime beyond them.

chapters.title: The saddle computes (3/p)
chapters.subtitle: heights that are Legendre symbols

lines.text: Slide every number round its own ring to the angle of its remainder after division by twenty-four. The primes gather on eight arms. Each is coloured by one question: is three a perfect square modulo that prime? Cyan if it is, magenta if not.
Now raise the saddle. Every cyan prime falls away, and every magenta prime rises. The height of each prime is the Legendre symbol of three, computed by the shape of the surface.
There are no exceptions among the primes up to two million. The reason is a single identity: the cosine of thirty degrees is half the square root of three.
Sixteen arms do the same for two. Primes one or seven more than a multiple of eight fall away; primes three or five more rise.
Ten arms compute five, but at two unequal heights, about plus zero point three and minus zero point eight: the two halves of the square root of five.
A hundred and forty-four arms on a twelve-fold saddle give the same answer for three: the forty-eight prime arms rise or fall by exactly the same amount.
The saddle's height is a cosine, and for these moduli a cosine is a Legendre symbol in disguise. It says which primes have three, two or five as a square, and nothing about which numbers are prime.

chapters.title: Base-12 fingerprints
chapters.subtitle: the last two digits of a curve

lines.text: Write a number in base twelve and keep its last two digits. There are a hundred and forty-four possible endings: a twelve by twelve board, the dozens digit down the side and the units digit across.
Every prime above three ends in one, five, seven or b, the four columns that share no factor with twelve. Here are the primes up to a million, filling exactly those columns.
A curve leaves its own fingerprint. The squares, one value at a time, light only sixteen cells, and just six of them in the prime columns.
Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one lights thirty-two cells, and every one of them is in a prime column. In base twelve its values end in five or b twice as often as in one or seven.
k squared plus k plus seventeen also stays inside the prime columns, through a different set of rows.
The pronic numbers never reach a prime column at all. A product of two neighbours is always even.
Side by side, the fingerprints show which remainders by two and three each curve avoids. That is all they can show: past three, the board is blind.

chapters.title: The 144 clock
chapters.subtitle: product families on the 24 half-hours

lines.text: Far from the centre, every curve straightens into a line pointing in a direction set by its middle coefficient. The directions that are whole multiples of a twenty-fourth of a turn are the hours of a clock.
On every hour lies a product family, u times q squared u plus d, where q squared divides a hundred and forty-four: one, four, nine, sixteen, thirty-six or a hundred and forty-four.
Fourteen hours hold no primes at all near their rays: the twelve even hours, and hours three and twenty-one.
The other ten hold a few primes, carried by quadratics that sit just beside the product family, like sixteen k squared plus eleven k plus two at hour nine.
On the saddle, the hours bend with the surface, and each family climbs or falls along it.
The clock's numbers are the square divisors of a hundred and forty-four. Twelve times twelve is the natural size for the primes two and three, and nothing in it can see beyond them.

chapters.title: Mirrors for prime pairs
chapters.subtitle: the curves without primes reflect the most

lines.text: Every number is a mirror. Step the same distance to either side of a number on the pronic ray, and the two numbers you land on sit symmetric across the ray.

When both are prime, they are a Goldbach pair: two primes that add up to twice the mirror, joined by a chord across the ray. Across thirty turns, from turn ten on, the pronic mirrors reflect fifty-four pairs.

Now Euler's line, k squared plus k plus forty-one, the most prime-rich curve on the spiral. Over the same thirty turns its mirrors reflect only sixteen pairs, and half of its mirrors reflect none at all.

Over two thousand turns the gap holds. The pronic mirrors reflect two point one five times as many prime pairs as Euler's, the squares one and a half times as many, and Euler's line is the weakest mirror of all.

The white ticks are a prediction, not a measurement. Hardy and Littlewood's form of Goldbach's conjecture multiplies a mirror's pairs by p minus one over p minus two for every odd prime p that divides it. The ticks land on the bars.

The reason is simple. When p divides the mirror, p can spoil a pair only when it also divides the step: one way instead of two. Pronic numbers are always even, and two times in three divisible by three. Euler's values have no prime factor below forty-one.
A chord is an unordered pair of angles, and the unordered pairs of points on a circle form a Möbius band. Its single edge is where the two angles meet.
Every chord of the squares and pronic mirrors lands on one rung of the band: the reflection across the x axis.
Euler's chords scatter over the whole band, because the direction of its mirror swings from one turn to the next.
So cancellation and anti-cancellation trade places. The curves that never hold a prime are the best mirrors for pairs of primes, and a mirror's own small factors predict how good it is.

chapters.title: The sieve machine
chapters.subtitle: Fermat's walk through rings of residues

lines.text: To factor a number n, Fermat looked for a square, a squared, that is n more than another square, b squared. Then n is a minus b times a plus b. The search starts at the first a whose square passes n.

Most a can be ruled out without taking a square root. Each ring is one modulus, from three to nineteen. Its gold holes are the residues of a where a squared minus n can still be a square; the dark ones are ruled out.
Step a by one, and every ring turns by one hole. Light from the centre runs out through the window until a closed ring stops it.
At a equals forty-nine every ring is open, and forty-nine squared minus fifteen hundred and one is nine hundred, thirty squared. So fifteen hundred and one is nineteen times seventy-nine.
One ring never closed. The ring for nineteen is gold all the way round, because nineteen divides fifteen hundred and one. For a prime ring, no dark holes means the prime is a factor.

For fifty thousand three hundred and ninety-nine, the light first escapes at a equals three hundred, the seventy-sixth candidate. Three hundred squared minus fifty thousand three hundred and ninety-nine is a hundred and ninety-nine squared, so it is a hundred and one times four hundred and ninety-nine.
Here is the record: one row per candidate, one column per ring. Only one row passes every column, and it is the answer.

D. H. Lehmer built sieves like this, first from bicycle chains, then in 1932 from gears and a photocell. They are fast when the two factors are close together. When the factors are far apart, a has to climb a long way, and the rings only shorten the climb by a constant factor.

chapters.title: Twisted tori
chapters.subtitle: a knot of residues and the umbilic torus

lines.text: Here is a different twist. Put each number n a seventh of a turn further around a torus, and a fifth of a turn further around its tube. The numbers wind a torus knot through thirty-five beads.
Every prime except five and seven lands on one of twenty-four beads. The other eleven beads lie on two red circles, the multiples of five on one and the multiples of seven on the other.
Euler's line visits only twelve of the twenty-four and never touches a red circle: its discriminant, minus a hundred and sixty-three, has no square root modulo five or seven.
This torus is the sieve machine with two rings: turning both by one notch steps along the knot. A torus of residues sorts the numbers; it cannot find a prime the residues have not already allowed.

Now wind the spiral itself around a torus, one lap per turn. This is Ferguson's umbilic torus. Its tube is a three-cornered deltoid that twists a third of a turn every lap, so its single edge runs around three times before it closes.
Cut at the squares ray, every cross-section has three positions, and turn k always lands in position k mod three. The turns sort into three stacks.
Then each curve meets three on whole stacks. k squared plus k plus one is a multiple of three on every turn of one stack, and all its primes sit on the other two.

k squared plus k plus three is the reverse: two stacks cancelled, and all eight of its primes on the third. A curve whose constant is two more than a multiple of three, like Euler's, is never cancelled by three at all.
Without the twist, every turn lies on the same face, and the cancelled values mix with the primes.

A half twist of a flat strip is a Möbius band, which sorts the turns by parity, and a tube with q corners sorts them mod q. The twisted shapes make residues visible, and that is all they do: the sorting is the residue lattice, drawn on a surface.

chapters.title: Two norm surfaces
chapters.subtitle: every curve is a slice of a bowl or a saddle

lines.text: Here are two surfaces: a bowl, x squared plus y squared, and a saddle, x squared minus y squared. They meet along one parabola, where y is zero: the squares.

Every curve on the spiral is a slice of one of them. Cut the bowl at a distance of root one sixty-three over two and read the heights at half steps: forty-one, forty-three, forty-seven. That is Euler's line.
Every curve with a negative discriminant is a slice of the bowl. k squared plus k plus seventeen lies at four point oh nine, and Landau's k squared plus one at one.

Curves with a positive discriminant are slices of the saddle. At a half-integer distance the slice factors: k times k plus one at one half, u times u plus four at two, u times u plus six at three. After their first value, every one is composite.
At an irrational distance the saddle's slices carry primes again. k squared plus k minus one, at root five over two, has seven primes among its first ten values.
The level curves hold the factorizations. On the saddle, x squared minus y squared equals thirteen passes through one point for each way to write thirteen as a times b. A prime has just four.
On the bowl the same height is a circle, the Sacks ring of thirteen, through its sums of two squares. Sixty-five, five times thirteen, has eight factor points and sixteen square points.
So the cancellation curves are the saddle's half-integer slices. The prime curves are everywhere else, and richest on the bowl.

chapters.title: Rings through lattices
chapters.subtitle: four classes of primes mod 12

lines.text: The Sacks ring of a number n is a circle of radius root n. Lay the square lattice and the triangular lattice under the ring of thirteen: it passes through eight square points, its sums of two squares, and twelve triangular ones.
Every prime falls into one of four patterns, set by its remainder mod twelve. Seventeen meets only the square lattice.
Nineteen meets only the triangular lattice: twelve points, and none on the square grid.
And twenty-three meets neither. Its ring threads between every point of both lattices.
For composite numbers the counts multiply. Eleven oh five, five times thirteen times seventeen, is the first ring with thirty-two square points.
Seventeen twenty-nine, seven times thirteen times nineteen, is the first with forty-eight triangular points. It is twelve cubed plus one.
Euler's lattice is long and thin: the integers along one row, and the next row at a height of root one sixty-three over two.
Euler's values are squared distances to that row. The ring of k squared plus k plus forty-one passes through the point k plus a half, for every k.
Forty rings in a row are prime. The forty-first is sixteen eighty-one, forty-one squared.

chapters.title: A twelve-dimensional torus
chapters.subtitle: 144 shadows of the sieve

lines.text: Write every number by its remainders modulo the first twelve primes, from two to thirty-seven. That makes it a point on a torus with twelve dimensions.
A twelve-dimensional torus casts a hundred and forty-four flat shadows, one for each pair of those primes. Each shadow is a grid of remainder pairs.
Below forty-one squared, a number above thirty-seven is prime exactly when it lands on no zero row and no zero column. The tour's spiral stops at sixteen oh one, inside that range.
Now follow Euler's line through all hundred and forty-four shadows. Its values light up a plaid of cells, and never a cross.
Minus one sixty-three is not a square modulo any prime up to thirty-seven, so none of them can divide k squared plus k plus forty-one.
The pronic numbers do the opposite. They land on both arms of every cross.
Close up on the first thirty-six shadows. Green is Euler's line, red the pronic numbers, and orange Landau's k squared plus one, which meets only the crosses of two, five and thirteen.
Twelve dimensions turn the sieve of Eratosthenes into a shape, and Euler's line is a curve that stays off every cross.

chapters.title: The modular surface
chapters.subtitle: points, closed geodesics and cusps

lines.text: Every curve k squared plus B k plus C has two roots. Put them in the upper half plane, where the modular group draws its tiling.

A curve with a negative discriminant has a pair of complex roots, so it becomes a single point. The squares side stands on the line through zero, and the pronic side on the left edge of the fundamental domain.
Landau's k squared plus one is the point i, and k squared plus k plus one is the corner rho. Euler's curve sits high on the left edge, at a height of root one sixty-three over two.
A curve with a positive discriminant has two real roots, joined by a semicircle: a geodesic.
When the discriminant is a perfect square, both roots are integers and the geodesic runs into two cusps. Those are the cancellation curves, in red.
Otherwise the geodesic closes up on the modular surface. k squared plus k minus one closes after a length of two log phi squared.
The floor of the fundamental domain is itself a cancellation geodesic, k squared minus one, and the points of Landau's curve and of k squared plus k plus one stand on it.

At the class-number-one points the j-invariant is a perfect cube: twelve cubed at i, zero at rho, and minus six hundred forty thousand three hundred twenty cubed at Euler's point. That is why e to the pi root one sixty-three is almost an integer.

chapters.title: The lattice race
chapters.subtitle: cosine waves of L-function zeros

lines.text: Primes whose rings miss the square lattice race against primes whose rings hit it: three mod four against one mod four.
Scaled by log x over root x, the gap hovers near two. The bias comes from prime squares: the square of every odd prime is one mod four.
The white curve rebuilds the race from that bias plus one cosine wave for each zero of Dirichlet's beta function, the L-function of the square lattice.
The waves dip to zero at twenty-six thousand eight hundred sixty-one, the first time the hits take the lead, and again near six hundred sixteen thousand and near twelve million.
Mod twelve, primes fall into four lattice classes: both lattices, square only, triangular only, and neither.
The class that meets both lattices has never led, up to a hundred million. The zeros of three L-functions rebuild each lane.
Its closest call is at forty-eight million two hundred thirty-one thousand seven hundred eighty-five, and the cosine waves put their lowest point at the same place.

chapters.title: Dropping onto E8
chapters.subtitle: prime or not prime, by position and by intersection

lines.text: E eight is a lattice in eight dimensions, built from symmetry alone: every coordinate whole, or every coordinate half-whole, with an even sum. Seen in its Coxeter plane, its two hundred and forty nearest points lie on eight rings of thirty.

One turn of its Coxeter element moves each ring a single step, a thirtieth of a circle. Thirty is two times three times five, and only eight of the thirty steps turn E eight the same way: one, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three and twenty-nine.
Drop every number onto the wheel at its step. Every prime above five lands on one of those eight spokes, so a number off them is divisible by two, three or five, and position alone has told us.
But forty-nine, seventy-seven and ninety-one land on the spokes as well. Position stops at thirty. For the rest, we drop through the lattice itself.

Take the sphere of radius root two n around the centre, and count the lattice points it passes through. For a prime, the count is two hundred and forty times one plus n cubed: the fewest a sphere can hold.
Four holds one thousand nine hundred and twenty more than that floor, two hundred and forty times two cubed, for its divisor two. Five is back on the floor.
Six holds eight thousand four hundred more: two cubed plus three cubed, times two hundred and forty. Seven sits on the floor again.
So every sphere counts cubes, one cube for each divisor. Seven has only the smallest cube and the largest. Six has cubes in between, and they are its factors.

For thirty-five, the extra cubes are five cubed plus seven cubed, four hundred and sixty-eight. That one count gives the factors back. It did so for all five thousand and eighty-one products of two primes below twenty thousand.

Nothing about primes went into E eight, only symmetry, yet one intersection, a sphere with the lattice, decides prime or not prime. The catch is that counting a sphere takes longer than trying the divisors. The symmetry knows the primes. It does not yet give a shortcut.

chapters.title: E5 to E8, from mirrors
chapters.subtitle: how the wheels are built

lines.text: Every symmetry in E eight is built from one move: a mirror. Reflect the plane in a line, and every point jumps to its image on the other side. The arrow at right angles to the mirror is called a root.

Two mirrors at sixty degrees make more. Reflect in one, then the other, and the plane turns by a third of a circle. Together they generate a third mirror, six images of any point, and six roots in a hexagon.

Two mirrors at right angles don't mix: they make just four images and four roots. So a set of mirrors can be drawn as a diagram: a dot for each mirror, a line between two that meet at sixty degrees, and no line where they're square.

The E series is one diagram that keeps growing. Five dots in a fork make E five. Add a dot to the end of an arm for E six, extend that arm again for E seven, and once more for E eight. A ninth dot would never close up: its mirrors would go on forever.

The diagram fixes every angle, and the mirrors generate all the roots: forty for E five, seventy-two for E six, a hundred and twenty-six for E seven, and two hundred and forty for E eight. Here they are, flattened onto their best plane.
Reflect in each mirror once, one after another, and the result is a single rotation, the Coxeter element. On that plane it turns every root by one step of a wheel.

The wheel has as many hours as roots divided by mirrors: forty over five is eight, seventy-two over six is twelve, a hundred and twenty-six over seven is eighteen, and two hundred and forty over eight is thirty.

Drop the counting numbers onto each wheel at their hour, and stack the four wheels. The gold spokes are the hours that share no factor with the wheel's size, so every prime that doesn't divide it lands on one.
actions: exp:say:E5, E6, E7, E8 stacked|8, 12, 18, 30 hours — gold spokes share no factor with the hour count

lines.text: Follow a number down through the stack. Nine sits on a spoke of E five, then falls off at E six, because three divides twelve. Fifteen does the same.
Twenty-five stays on a spoke through E five, E six and E seven, and falls off at E eight: thirty is the only wheel size with a factor of five. Thirty-five does the same.
But forty-nine, seventy-seven and ninety-one stay on a spoke in all four. Eight, twelve, eighteen and thirty are built from two, three and five, so no E wheel can ever remove seven.
actions: delay:2.6:exp:say:49, 77 and 91:  on all four|8, 12, 18 and 30 are built from 2, 3 and 5:  none removes 7

lines.text: So the mirrors of E five to E eight sort out the multiples of two, three and five, and stop there. The primes beyond that need a different map.
actions: exp:say:the mirrors sort out 2, 3 and 5|and stop there — no E-wheel removes 7

chapters.title: The paths back
chapters.subtitle: prime factors and their exponents

lines.text: Now lift E eight's wheel into three dimensions. Every number up to four hundred gets a column as tall as its logarithm, so every column reaches the same funnel.
actions: exp:say:every number gets a column|as tall as its logarithm

lines.text: Cut each column into one piece per prime factor, each as tall as the log of its prime: red for two, green for three, blue for five, orange for seven, and gold for the large primes.
actions: exp:say:one piece per prime factor|red 2, green 3, blue 5, orange 7, violet 11, cyan 13, gold 17 and up

lines.text: A prime's column is a single piece. Three ninety-seven is prime: one gold segment, and one drop straight down to one.

Three hundred sixty is two cubed, times three squared, times five. Start at the top of its column. Divide by two: drop one red segment and step across to the column of one eighty, which is exactly that tall.
Divide by two again, to ninety, and again, to forty-five. Three equal red drops in a row: two has exponent three.
Now the green drops: forty-five divided by three is fifteen, and fifteen by three is five. Two green drops make three squared. One blue drop takes five to one.
Two hundred fifty-six is two to the eighth: eight equal red drops, spiralling down the funnel through one twenty-eight, sixty-four, thirty-two, and on to one.
Three forty-three is seven cubed: three orange drops, through forty-nine and seven. Each is longer than a drop of two, because seven is a larger prime.
Two hundred ten is two times three times five times seven: four colours, one drop each. Every exponent is one.
Three twenty-four is two squared times three to the fourth: two red drops, then four green ones.

Laid side by side, the paths read like a score. The length of each drop names the prime, and the number of equal drops in a row is its exponent. By unique factorization, every number has exactly one such set of drops.
actions: exp:say:the paths, side by side|each drop names a prime — equal drops in a row are its exponent

lines.text: The catch is that drawing a path needs the factors first. Finding them from the number alone is the hard problem that keeps internet encryption safe.
actions: exp:say:the path is the factorization|finding it from n alone is the hard problem behind RSA

chapters.title: The zeros inside E8's stack
chapters.subtitle: where zeta's zeros live, and how E8 sorts the primes

lines.text: Here is E eight's factor funnel again. Every number up to four hundred stands at its hour on the wheel, with a column as tall as its logarithm. So where, in this stack, are the zeros of zeta?
actions: exp:say:where are ζ's zeros in the stack?|every n at its hour, its column as tall as log n

lines.text: Not at any point. At a zero, one half plus i gamma, every number n is turned by gamma times log n: its height in the funnel, times gamma. So a zero is a coil wound up the axis. The first zero, fourteen point one three, turns once every point four four of height.
actions: exp:say:a zero is a coil up the axis|n turns by γ·log n — its height times γ

lines.text: The second and third zeros, twenty-one point zero two and twenty-five point zero one, are tighter coils. And every drop of a path back, dividing by a prime p, lowers the height by log p and turns every coil by gamma times log p.

Now take all ten thousand five hundred zeros and look at one height: where seven sits. Their coils lean towards minus one. On average, by minus point one one five, which is exactly what Landau's formula predicts for a prime.
actions: exp:say:at the height of 7, a prime|10 500 coils lean to −1: mean −0.115, Landau −0.115

lines.text: At the height of six, two times three, the coils point every way, and their mean is zero. The zeros lean only at prime powers.
actions: exp:say:at the height of 6 = 2·3|the coils cancel: mean 0.000

lines.text: So add up all the coils at every height, together with zeta's pole, and draw the sum out to the side. What is left is a comb: a tooth of exactly log p at every prime power, reaching the top of that prime's column, and nothing at the composites.
actions: exp:say:added up, the coils light every prime power|a tooth of log p, reaching the top of p's column

lines.text: But the comb is the same in every direction. Spin it round the axis, and each tooth becomes a ring through its prime's column. Zeta's zeros know how high a prime sits, but not its hour on the wheel.
actions: exp:say:spun round the axis: a ring per prime power|ζ's zeros fix the height, not the hour

lines.text: E eight knows more. Its Coxeter element makes E eight a lattice over the thirtieth roots of unity, and their field has eight L-functions, one for each character of E eight's exponent group. Zeta is the first.
actions: exp:say:E8's field has eight L-functions|one per character of (Z/30)*, E8's exponents — ζ is the first

lines.text: The zeros of each one light the same prime powers, but turned by the character: back and forth for the real ones, and all four ways for the others. Every tooth of one colour, one hour, points the same way.
actions: exp:say:each turns the primes by χ(p)|±1 for the real characters, ±1 and ±i for the rest

lines.text: Now turn each set of zeros back by its character at hour h, and add all eight. Only the primes on spoke h survive. Spoke one. Seven. Eleven. Thirteen. Seventeen. Nineteen. Twenty-three. Twenty-nine.
actions: exp:say:turned back by χ(h) and added|only the primes on spoke h survive

lines.text: Seven thousand four hundred zeros, none higher than a thousand, sort every prime up to four hundred onto its spoke. Zeta's zeros give the height. The other seven give the hour.
actions: exp:say:7 420 zeros up to t = 1000|ζ's give the height, the other seven the hour

lines.text: And the paths back walk through these lamps. Three sixty drops log two three times, log three twice, and log five once. Each drop is exactly the sum of the zeros at a prime power dividing it: two cubed, two squared, two, three squared, three and five. At the stops in between, the zeros cancel.
actions: exp:say:every drop is a lamp the zeros light|log n = Σ Λ(d) over the prime powers d dividing n

lines.text: Among themselves, the zeros of each L-function repel, like the eigenvalues of a random unitary matrix. Zeros of different L-functions ignore each other. E eight's field holds eight independent spectra.
actions: exp:say:within one L-function: repulsion|between the eight: none — eight independent spectra

lines.text: So the zeros are not points in the stack. They are frequencies of its height. Added up, they rebuild the prime powers. Turned by E eight's characters, they put each prime on its spoke. They reconstruct the primes, but they do not predict them.
actions: exp:say:the zeros are frequencies of the height|they rebuild the primes — they do not predict them

chapters.title: Five discoveries
chapters.subtitle: what this search found, and why it matters

lines.text: This search began with a spiral of numbers and one question: what geometry hides in the primes? Five findings stood out. For each one, here is what we found, why it matters, and what is new.
actions: exp:say:five discoveries|what this search found, and why it matters

lines.text: One. The saddle under the spiral is a wave. We bent the Sacks spiral over a saddle to make its curves stand out. The saddle rises and falls twice on every turn, the same rhythm as the first wave of Voronoi's formula for counting divisors.
actions: exp:say:1.  the saddle is a wave|the first wave of Voronoi's divisor formula:  two crests per turn

lines.text: Count points in circles instead of under hyperbolas, and the waves rise once per turn. They need the saddle twisted half a turn for every turn of the spiral. Two counting problems, two surfaces under one spiral.
actions: exp:say:circles:  one crest per turn|Hardy's waves ride the saddle twisted half a turn per turn

lines.text: Why it matters: the curves on the Sacks spiral are products, and these waves are how the count of products wobbles. Voronoi and Hardy found the formulas a century ago. What is new is seeing them as the surfaces beneath the spiral.
actions: exp:say:why it matters|the surface that shows the products is the products' own wave

lines.text: Two. Add one over n to the s, arrow by arrow, at a zero of zeta. The chain curls into vortices, one for every counting number, each the reflection of the chain's own start.
actions: exp:say:2.  the vortices of the zeta chain|one vortex for every counting number

lines.text: Keep only the numbers on E eight's eight gold hours, and each vortex carries a charge. Measured at height five thousand, the charges are the traces of E eight's Coxeter element: minus one, one, two, four, and so on, set only by the common factor with thirty.
actions: exp:say:the charges are E8's Coxeter traces|tr C<sup>k</sup> = −1, 1, 2, 4, −2, −4, −8, 8, set by gcd(k, 30)

lines.text: Why it matters: E eight's Coxeter trace is the sieve of two, three and five, written as a spectrum. So a Lie group sets the strength of every vortex. The identity behind it is Ramanujan's; what is new is watching E eight decide the vortices of zeta's chain.
actions: exp:say:why it matters|a Lie group sets the strength of each vortex

lines.text: Three. Where are zeta's zeros inside E eight? Not at points. Each zero is a coil wound up the factor funnel, and together the coils light every prime power. Zeta's zeros fix a prime's height; the zeros of seven more L-functions of E eight's field fix its spoke.
actions: exp:say:3.  where the zeros live in E8|coils up the funnel;  eight L-functions put each prime on its spoke

lines.text: E eight also has its own zeta function. Count its vectors by length, and you get two hundred and forty times zeta of s, times zeta of s minus three. Its critical line is real part two, and no zero sits on it: they lie on one half and on seven halves, mirror images.
actions: exp:say:E8's own zeta function|240 ζ(s) ζ(s − 3):  no zero on its own critical line, Re s = 2

lines.text: Why it matters: Riemann's zeros are E eight's own zeros, twice, and not one of them lies on E eight's own critical line. The formula is classical, Hecke's. The empty critical line is the picture this search adds.
actions: exp:say:why it matters|ζ's zeros are E8's own zeros, twice, all off its line

lines.text: Four: what the Riemann hypothesis depends on. Discriminant minus twenty-three has three families of curves, each with its own zeta function and Riemann's symmetry. Yet they have zeros off the critical line, one even at real part one point zero zero seven, where no Euler product can vanish.
actions: exp:say:4.  what keeps zeros on the line|each family's own zeta function has zeros off it

lines.text: Mix the families. Every mixture shares the functional equation, and one curve holds all their zeros on the line at once. Counted in full, up to height fifty, only two small windows of mixtures keep every zero on the line, both around the class group's L-functions.
actions: exp:say:every mixture at once|no zero off the line only round the two L-functions

lines.text: With five families, for minus forty-seven, the mixtures fill a plane. Colour each one by its zeros off the line, and gold appears only in small islands: around the three L-functions, and one more island with no L-function in it.
actions: exp:say:five families:  a plane of mixtures|gold:  no zero off the line up to t = 50

lines.text: Why it matters: symmetry alone does not put zeros on the line. Davenport and Heilbronn proved that in 1936. The functions that keep them there, as far as anyone has checked, are the ones with Euler products. What is new is seeing every mixture at once.
actions: exp:say:why it matters|symmetry alone does not keep zeros on the line

lines.text: Five: the prime race. Race the primes on E eight's eight spokes up to ten million. Spokes one and nineteen run three behind, ahead of their share only zero point three and one point four percent of the time, and six thousand seven hundred and seventy-one zeros rebuild every curve.
actions: exp:say:5.  the prime race on E8's spokes|spokes 1 and 19 run three behind

lines.text: The reason is a fold. The zeros count prime powers, and squaring folds the eight spokes onto one and nineteen, so every prime square lands there. Put the squares back, and the race is fair.
actions: exp:say:the reason:  a fold|squaring sends every spoke to 1 or 19

lines.text: The same fold decides another race: the families of minus twenty-three. Each prime acts on the roots of x cubed minus x minus one as a symmetry of a triangle. Every reflection squares to the identity, so the principal family runs three behind and never leads, up to ten million.
actions: exp:say:the same fold in S<sub>3</sub>|every reflection squares to the identity

lines.text: Why it matters: Chebyshev saw the bias in 1853, and Rubinstein and Sarnak explained it with the zeros. What is new is one picture for both races: when four elements square to the identity, the identity's class falls three behind.
actions: exp:say:why it matters|one fold for both races

lines.text: None of this finds primes faster than a sieve, and none of it proves the Riemann hypothesis. What the search found is geometry: a surface, a Lie group, a plane of mixtures and a fold, where classical facts that looked separate turn out to be one picture.
actions: exp:say:five discoveries|a surface, a Lie group, a plane of mixtures and a fold

chapters.title: The saddle is a wave
chapters.subtitle: discovery 1 of 5:  two master waves on the Sacks spiral

lines.text: Claude, an AI math research assistant, and I set out to find the geometry hidden in the counting numbers. This is where it leads: the Sacks spiral on its saddle, carrying the master wave of zeta's zeros, which spikes at every prime, and the curve of zeta rising out of the saddle's centre, touching its axis at every zero. Here is how it is built.
actions: exp:say:where this leads|ζ's master wave on the Sacks spiral  ·  ζ's curve rising from the saddle's centre

lines.text: We begin with the plainest picture: the counting numbers on a line, one dot for each. A prime can be divided only by one and itself. Two, three, five and seven are prime, and so are eleven and thirteen, in gold. Four is two times two, six is two times three, nine is three times three: those are not.

lines.text: Seven is a prime, and it has a spike. Eight is two cubed, a power of two, and it has one too; so does nine, three squared. But ten, two times five, has no spike, and neither does twelve, two squared times three.
actions: exp:say:spikes at the primes and prime powers|and nowhere else

lines.text: This is the cosine wave of the home view, drawn the way a mathematician would draw it, along the number line. It is the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt: added up, the zeros spike exactly at the prime powers.
actions: exp:say:the prime master wave|10 000 zeros:  the explicit formula, on the number line

lines.text: Now curl the number line up, one full turn for each step of the square root. Watch the graph curl with it: each number keeps its place along the line, and one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, the squares, come to rest on a single ray. This is the Sacks spiral.
actions: exp:say:curling the line|one turn for each step of √n:  the Sacks spiral

On that line every zero's wave swells like the square root of n, the radius of this very spiral, while every term of zeta shrinks like one over it. chapters.title: E8 sets the vortices
chapters.subtitle: discovery 2 of 5:  E8's clock inside zeta's path of partial sums

lines.text: Discovery two. Claude and I drew zeta's series as a path of partial sums: one arrow for every counting number n, one over root n long, each turning from the last by t times the logarithm of n over n minus one.

lines.text: Raise t, and the path climbs its axis, winding up as it goes; the grid below is the ground, where t is zero. At the first zero, t equal to fourteen point one three, the path's end lands on zero. chapters.title: Where the zeros live in E8
chapters.subtitle: discovery 3 of 5:  a zero is a coil up E8's factor funnel

lines.text: Discovery three. Claude and I asked where zeta's zeros live in E eight's layout of the counting numbers. Here it is: every number up to four hundred at its hour on E eight's wheel of thirty, with a column as tall as its logarithm, cut at its prime factors.
actions: exp:say:E8's factor funnel|n at its hour n mod 30, its column as tall as log n, cut at its prime factors
lines.caption: Discovery three. Claude and I asked where zeta's zeros live in {E8's|E eight's} layout of the counting numbers. Here it is: every number up to {400|four hundred} at its hour on {E8's|E eight's} wheel of {30|thirty}, with a column as tall as its logarithm, cut at its prime factors.

lines.text: That is too much at once, so grey it out and light one number at a time. Seven is a prime: its arm points to hour seven on the floor, and its column is one piece, log seven tall. Six is two times three, at hour six: a piece log three tall, and on top of it one log two tall.
actions: exp:say:one number at a time|7:  prime, one piece log 7   ·   6 = 2·3:  log 3 + log 2
lines.caption: That is too much at once, so grey it out and light one number at a time. Seven is a prime: its arm points to hour {7|seven} on the floor, and its column is one piece, {log 7|log seven} tall. {6 = 2 · 3,|Six is two times three,} at hour {6|six}: a piece {log 3|log three} tall, and on top of it one {log 2|log two} tall.

lines.text: Now bring in the path of partial sums from discovery two, at the first zero, t equal to fourteen point one three, and lay it on the funnel's floor, starting at the axis. Its arrows wind round and its tail brings it back to the axis.
actions: exp:say:the path at the first zero, on the floor|t = 14.13:  its arrows n<sup>−½ − it</sup> close on the axis
lines.caption: Now bring in the path of partial sums from discovery two, at the first zero, {t =|t equal to} {14.13|fourteen point one three}, and lay it on the funnel's floor, starting at the axis. Its arrows wind round and its tail brings it back to the axis.

lines.text: Lift each arrow to the height of its own number. Arrow n rises to log n, the top of n's column; its tail moves onto the axis, and it keeps both its direction and its length, one over root n. Arrow one stays on the floor, arrow two rises to log two, arrow six to log six: stacked, the shrinking arrows narrow like a horn.

Arrow n rises to log n, the top of n's column; its tail moves onto the axis, and it keeps both its direction and its length, {1/√n|one over root n}. Arrow one stays on the floor, arrow two rises to {log 2|log two}, arrow six to {log 6|log six}: stacked, the shrinking arrows narrow like a horn.

lines.text: Now stretch each arrow by the square root of its number: the distance of n from the centre on the Sacks spiral, and on this funnel's floor. One over root n, times root n, is one. On the critical line the length and the radius cancel, every arrow becomes one unit long, and all that is left is its direction.
actions: exp:say:stretch arrow n by √n|1/√n × √n = 1:  the critical line's ½ cancels the spiral's radius
delay:11.21:exp:say:every arrow one unit long|n<sup>−½</sup> · n<sup>½</sup> = 1:  only the direction γ·log n is left
lines.caption: Now stretch each arrow by the square root of its number: the distance of n from the centre on the Sacks spiral, and on this funnel's floor. {1/√n × √n = 1.|One over root n, times root n, is one.} On the critical line the length and the radius cancel, every arrow becomes one unit long, and all that is left is its direction.

lines.text: Stacked, the arrows are the hands of a clock that turns by gamma for every unit of height, and a coil runs through their tips, one turn every point four four. That coil is the zero, wound up E eight's funnel.
actions: exp:say:a zero is a coil|one turn every 2π/γ = 0.44 of height
lines.caption: Stacked, the arrows are the hands of a clock that turns by {γ|gamma} for every unit of height, and a coil runs through their tips, one turn every {0.44|point four four}. That coil is the zero, wound up {E8's|E eight's} funnel.

lines.text: And the coil reads the prime factors. Six is two times three, so log six is log two plus log three, and the hand at six has turned the turn of two plus the turn of three.
actions: exp:say:the hand of 6 = the hand of 2 + the hand of 3|γ·log 6 = γ·log 2 + γ·log 3:  1.56 + 2.47 = 4.03 turns
lines.caption: And the coil reads the prime factors. {6 = 2 · 3,|Six is two times three,} so {log 6 = log 2 + log 3,|log six is log two plus log three,} and the hand at six has turned the turn of two plus the turn of three.

lines.text: Every zero is such a coil. The next two, twenty-one point zero two and twenty-five point zero one, turn every hand further, the higher ones more: tighter coils.

lines.text: Now add the coils of all ten thousand five hundred zeros. A ring climbs the funnel's axis, and at each height the coils add up to a single hand. Where they agree, at a prime or a power of a prime, the hand shoots out to the top of that prime's column: seven, eight, nine. At six and ten they cancel, and the hand stays at the axis.
actions: exp:say:adding the coils, height by height|where they agree, a tooth of log p;  elsewhere they cancel

lines.caption: Climbing on, the ring lights every prime power up to {400|four hundred}, and leaves every composite dark. The comb it draws is the master wave of discovery one, stood up along the logarithm.

lines.text: Zeta's zeros fix a prime's height but not its hour. E eight's field has seven more L-functions; turned back by their characters, they split the comb into eight fans, one for each gold hour. Forty-nine, seven squared, lands on hour nineteen.
actions: exp:say:eight L-functions, eight spokes|ζ's zeros give the height, the other seven the hour
lines.caption: Zeta's zeros fix a prime's height but not its hour. {E8's|E eight's} field has seven more L-functions; turned back by their characters, they split the comb into eight fans, one for each gold hour. {49 = 7² lands on hour 19.|Forty-nine, seven squared, lands on hour nineteen.}

lines.text: Why it matters: the zeros are not points in E eight's stack. They are frequencies of its height, and every coil reads the prime factors. The explicit formula is classical; what Claude and I add is where each zero sits in E eight's funnel.
actions: exp:say:what is new|a zero is a coil up E8's funnel, turning with the logarithm of every number

chapters.title: What keeps zeros on the line
chapters.subtitle: discovery 4 of 5:  symmetry is not enough

lines.text: Discovery four. Discriminant minus twenty-three has three families of quadratic forms, and each family is a lattice of points. A number lies on a family when some point of its lattice sits at that number's distance squared from the centre.
actions: exp:say:three families, three lattices|x² + xy + 6y²  ·  2x² + xy + 3y²  ·  2x² − xy + 3y²
lines.caption: Discovery four. Discriminant {−23|minus twenty-three} has three families of quadratic forms, and each family is a lattice of points. A number lies on a family when some point of its lattice sits at that number's distance squared from the centre.

lines.text: Fifty-nine, a prime, lies on the first family only. Thirteen, a prime, lies on the other two. But six, two times three, lies on all three: a composite shows up on more than one family.
lines.caption: {59|Fifty-nine}, a prime, lies on the first family only. {13|Thirteen}, a prime, lies on the other two. But {6 = 2·3|six, two times three,} lies on all three: a composite shows up on more than one family.

lines.text: Now count the points on each ring. On the second family, two has two points, and three has two points.
actions: exp:say:count the points on each ring|2x² + xy + 3y²:  2 has 2 points,  3 has 2 points

lines.text: On the first family, two and three have no points at all. But six, two times three, has four.
actions: exp:say:count the points on each ring|x² + xy + 6y²:  2 has none,  3 has none,  6 = 2·3 has 4
lines.caption: On the first family, two and three have no points at all. But {6 = 2·3|six, two times three,} has four.

lines.text: So the first family's counts cannot be built from the prime factors: zero times zero is not four. But take the first family's count minus the second's, and halve it. Two gives minus one, three gives minus one, and six gives plus one, which is minus one times minus one. Building every count from its prime factors is exactly what an Euler product does: zeta's own product over the primes.
actions: exp:say:counts built from the prime factors|(first − second)/2:  6 → +1 = (−1) × (−1):  an Euler product
lines.caption: So the first family's counts cannot be built from the prime factors: {0 × 0 ≠ 4.|zero times zero is not four.} But take the first family's count minus the second's, and halve it. {2 → −1,|Two gives minus one,} {3 → −1,|three gives minus one,} and {6 → +1 = (−1) × (−1).|six gives plus one, which is minus one times minus one.} Building every count from its prime factors is exactly what an Euler product does: zeta's own product over the primes.

lines.text: Each family has its own zeta function, counting its lattice points by distance, with Riemann's symmetry. The lattices move up to head their strips of zeros. Yet those zeros leave the critical line; one sits at real part one point zero zero seven, where no function with an Euler product can vanish.
actions: exp:say:each family's own zeta function|red: zeros off the critical line Re s = ½
lines.caption: Each family has its own zeta function, counting its lattice points by distance, with Riemann's symmetry. The lattices move up to head their strips of zeros. Yet those zeros leave the critical line; one sits at real part {1.007|one point zero zero seven}, where no function with an Euler product can vanish.

lines.text: The two combinations of the families with Euler products keep every zero on the line: forty-four and forty-two zeros, all gold.
actions: exp:say:the class group's L-functions|(Z<sub>1</sub> + 2Z<sub>2</sub>)/2 and (Z<sub>1</sub> − Z<sub>2</sub>)/2:  every zero on the line
lines.caption: The two combinations of the families with Euler products keep every zero on the line: {44|forty-four} and {42|forty-two} zeros, all gold.

lines.text: Now the curves of the chart, built step by step. On the critical line each family's completed zeta function is a real wave: gold for the first family, blue for the second. Their zeros are where the waves cross the axis.
actions: exp:say:each family on the critical line|Λ(½ + it) is real:  gold x² + xy + 6y²,  blue 2x² ± xy + 3y²

lines.text: Mix them: the first plus lambda times the second. That mixture is zero where the first equals minus lambda times the second, that is, where the ratio, minus the first over the second, equals lambda. Sweep along t and plot that ratio: wherever the blue wave crosses zero it divides by zero and shoots off to infinity, so the curve breaks into these branches.

That mixture is zero where the first equals minus {λ|lambda} times the second, that is, where the ratio, minus the first over the second, equals {λ|lambda}. Sweep along t and plot that ratio: wherever the blue wave crosses zero it divides by zero and shoots off to infinity, so the curve breaks into these branches.

At zero it meets the gold dots, the first family's own zeros. {At λ = 2 and λ = −1|At two and at minus one} it meets the two L-functions with Euler products, and every one of their zeros is there.

lines.text: With five families, for minus forty-seven, there are two weights instead of one, and the mixtures fill a plane. Build it row by row: each row is a sweep like the one we just made, every cell coloured by how many zeros leave the line, gold where none do.
actions: exp:say:five families:  a plane of mixtures|Λ<sub>1</sub> + λ<sub>2</sub>Λ<sub>2</sub> + λ<sub>3</sub>Λ<sub>3</sub>:  every row a sweep
lines.caption: With five families, for {−47|minus forty-seven}, there are two weights instead of one, and the mixtures fill a plane. Build it row by row: each row is a sweep like the one we just made, every cell coloured by how many zeros leave the line, gold where none do.

lines.text: Now raise every mixture by its number of zeros off the line, and the plane becomes a landscape. The gold patches are its valleys, at sea level. Slice through it, and each slice is a sweep like minus twenty-three's: where it dips to the floor, a window.

lines.caption: Now raise every mixture by its number of zeros off the line, and the plane becomes a landscape. The gold patches are its valleys, at sea level. Slice through it, and each slice is a sweep like {−23's:|minus twenty-three's:} where it dips to the floor, a window.

lines.text: Three valleys surround the class group's three L-functions, and their counts, like minus twenty-three's, are built from their prime factors: Euler products. One more valley has no L-function in it.
actions: exp:say:the valleys|round the three L-functions:  Euler products,  counts built from primes
lines.caption: Three valleys surround the class group's three L-functions, and their counts, like {−23's,|minus twenty-three's,} are built from their prime factors: Euler products. One more valley has no L-function in it.

lines.text: Why it matters: symmetry alone does not keep zeros on the line. Davenport and Heilbronn proved that in nineteen thirty-six. As far as anyone has checked, the functions that keep them there are the ones whose counts are built from their prime factors: the Euler products. What Claude and I add is seeing every mixture at once.

What Claude and I add is seeing every mixture at once.

All eight gold hours, squared, land on {1|one} or {19|nineteen}: the only two square hours on the clock.

lines.text: Follow one prime's powers round the clock, the radius growing with the logarithm. Seven sits on hour seven. Seven squared, forty-nine, on nineteen. Seven cubed, three hundred and forty-three, on thirteen. Seven to the fourth, two thousand four hundred and one, back on hour one. Every even power lands on one or nineteen.

Every even power lands on {1|one} or {19|nineteen}.

lines.text: The same fold turns up in a second race. For minus twenty-three, a prime's family is decided by how many roots x cubed minus x minus one has among the numbers modulo that prime. Take five: five numbers, zero to four. Put each one in. Only two gives a multiple of five, eight minus two minus one: one root.

For {−23|minus twenty-three}, a prime's family is decided by how many roots {x³ − x − 1|x cubed minus x minus one} has among the numbers modulo that prime. Take five: five numbers, zero to four. Put each one in. Only two gives a multiple of five, {8 − 2 − 1:|eight minus two minus one:} one root.

lines.text: Those counts tell how the prime moves the three roots of x cubed minus x minus one. Three roots fixed: the identity, nothing moves. No root fixed: a rotation, all three move round. One root fixed: a reflection, the mirror: one root stays and the other two swap.
