chapters.title: The path of partial sums
chapters.subtitle: the zeros inside E8, part 1:  how ζ is built, link by link

lines.text: Claude, an AI math research assistant, and I set out to find where the zeros of zeta live among the counting numbers. First, a refresher on how zeta is built: one arrow for every counting number, laid end to end. Mathematicians call this the path of partial sums.
actions: exp:say:the path of partial sums|ζ(s) = 1 + 1/2<sup>s</sup> + 1/3<sup>s</sup> + …,  one arrow per term

lines.text: Take the height t equal to one. The first arrow is one unit long and points to the right. The second is one over the square root of two long, and it turns away from the first by the logarithm of two: forty degrees.
lines.caption: Take the height {t = 1.|t equal to one.} The first arrow is one unit long and points to the right. The second is {1/√2|one over the square root of two} long, and it turns away from the first by {log 2:|the logarithm of two:} {40°.|forty degrees.}

lines.text: The third is one over root three long, and turns a further log of three halves, twenty-three degrees. Its direction is the sum of the turns: log three, sixty-three degrees from the first. Every direction is a logarithm.
lines.caption: The third is {1/√3|one over root three} long, and turns a further {log(3/2), 23°.|log of three halves, twenty-three degrees.} Its direction is the sum of the turns: {log 3 = 63°|log three, sixty-three degrees} from the first. Every direction is a logarithm.

lines.text: Four, five, six, seven, eight: shorter and shorter arrows, turning less and less, seventeen degrees, then thirteen, ten, nine and eight, because the logarithm climbs more and more slowly.
lines.caption: Four, five, six, seven, eight: shorter and shorter arrows, turning less and less, {17°, 13°, 10°, 9° and 8°,|seventeen degrees, then thirteen, ten, nine and eight,} because the logarithm climbs more and more slowly.

lines.text: Now raise the height t. Every angle is t times a logarithm, so the path winds up tighter. The arrows go on forever, but past a point the rest add up to a simple tail, drawn in orange, and the end of that tail is zeta of one half plus i t.
actions: exp:say:raising t|every angle is t × a logarithm;  the tail adds all the arrows beyond
lines.caption: Now raise the height t. Every angle is t times a logarithm, so the path winds up tighter. The arrows go on forever, but past a point the rest add up to a simple tail, drawn in orange, and the end of that tail is {ζ(½ + it).|zeta of one half plus i t.}

lines.text: At t equal to fourteen point one three, the end lands exactly on zero. That is the first zero of zeta: all the arrows, from one to infinity, cancel out.
lines.caption: At {t =|t equal to} {14.13|fourteen point one three}, the end lands exactly on zero. That is the first zero of zeta: all the arrows, from one to infinity, cancel out.

lines.text: Now let t run on, and stand the plane up on a t axis, so that it climbs as t grows. The end of the path leaves a trail, the curve of zeta along the critical line. It touches the axis at every zero: twenty-one point zero two, twenty-five point zero one, thirty point four two.
actions: exp:say:the curve of ζ on the critical line|the plane climbs the t axis;  the curve touches it at every zero
lines.caption: Now let t run on, and stand the plane up on a t axis, so that it climbs as t grows. The end of the path leaves a trail, the curve of zeta along the critical line. It touches the axis at every zero: {21.02|twenty-one point zero two}, {25.01|twenty-five point zero one}, {30.42|thirty point four two}.

lines.text: Between the zeros, the curve swings out and comes back. Riemann's hypothesis says that every zero of this kind lies on this line, real part one half. Trillions have been checked, and every one does, but no one has proved that all of them must.
actions: exp:say:Riemann's hypothesis|every nontrivial zero of ζ has real part ½
lines.caption: Between the zeros, the curve swings out and comes back. Riemann's hypothesis says that every zero of this kind lies on this line, {Re s = ½.|real part one half.} Trillions have been checked, and every one does, but no one has proved that all of them must.

lines.text: Higher up, the path needs more and more arrows before the tail takes over, and it begins to curl into knots. Those knots are its vortices, and the next part follows them up the axis.
actions: exp:say:the vortices begin|knots in the path, ringed

chapters.title: How the vortices develop
chapters.subtitle: the zeros inside E8, part 2:  the path of partial sums high up

lines.text: Climbing higher, the path needs about t over pi arrows before its tail takes over, and it curls into knots: vortices. The rings mark their eyes, numbered from the far end of the path.
actions: exp:say:vortices|about t/2π of them at height t

lines.text: Each time t over two pi passes another whole number, a new vortex is born near the start of the path, and the older ones move out along it.
actions: exp:say:a vortex is born|each time t/2π passes a whole number

lines.text: Between the vortices the path runs straight. Those straight runs are the spokes, where each arrow turns by a whole number of full turns from the last. They sit near n equal to t over two pi k: at the hundred and fifty-ninth zero, fifty-three, twenty-seven and eighteen.
actions: exp:say:spoke k at n ≈ t / 2πk|where each arrow turns a whole number of turns from the last
lines.caption: Between the vortices the path runs straight. Those straight runs are the spokes, where each arrow turns by a whole number of full turns from the last. They sit near {n ≈ t/2πk:|n equal to t over two pi k:} at the {159th|hundred and fifty-ninth} zero, {53|fifty-three}, {27|twenty-seven} and {18|eighteen}.

lines.text: Each vortex has an eye, and each eye is a mirror image: the path's own kay-th vertex, reflected through zeta's phase. The crosses mark those mirror points, and they land inside the rings.
actions: exp:say:every eye is a mirror|eye of vortex k = the path's k-th vertex, reflected through ζ's phase
lines.caption: Each vortex has an eye, and each eye is a mirror image: the path's own {k-th|kay-th} vertex, reflected through zeta's phase. The crosses mark those mirror points, and they land inside the rings.

lines.text: Now unwind the path onto the number line. Every arrow drops onto its own counting number, in the colour of its vortex. Vortex one lands between twenty-seven and fifty-three, vortex two between eighteen and twenty-seven, vortex three between thirteen and eighteen. Each stretch is shorter than the last, and below seven the vortices are smaller than one arrow: a tangle.
actions: exp:say:the vortices on the number line|the 159th zero:  vortex k on the arrows from t/2π(k + 1) to t/2πk
lines.caption: Now unwind the path onto the number line. Every arrow drops onto its own counting number, in the colour of its vortex. Vortex one lands between {27|twenty-seven} and {53|fifty-three}, vortex two between {18|eighteen} and {27|twenty-seven}, vortex three between {13|thirteen} and {18|eighteen}. Each stretch is shorter than the last, and below seven the vortices are smaller than one arrow: a tangle.

lines.text: Now the mirror that puts each eye in place: arrow n goes to t over two pi n, here fifty-three over n. On the mirror's side, vortex one fills the stretch from one to two, vortex two from two to three: lined up on one axis, the vortices are evenly spaced, one for every counting number. The two sides meet at the square root of fifty-three, seven point three.
actions: exp:say:the mirror:  n → t/2πn|vortex k fills the stretch from k to k + 1:  one vortex for every counting number
delay:23.37:exp:say:the fold:  √(t/2π) = 7.3|the arrows before it make the tangle;  the arrows after it make the vortices
lines.caption: Now the mirror that puts each eye in place: arrow n goes to {t/2πn,|t over two pi n,} here {53/n.|fifty-three over n.} On the mirror's side, vortex one fills the stretch from one to two, vortex two from two to three: lined up on one axis, the vortices are evenly spaced, one for every counting number. The two sides meet at {√53 = 7.3.|the square root of fifty-three, seven point three.}

lines.text: Slide the mirror's side onto the line, and the colours read the same both ways from seven point three: one counting number for each vortex on one side, its long stretch of arrows on the other. Wind the line into the Sacks spiral, and the fold becomes a circle: inside it the first seven counting numbers, outside it the vortices, bands of the spiral that widen toward the rim.
actions: exp:say:the vortices on the Sacks spiral|the fold is a circle:  counting numbers inside, vortices outside, the same colours
lines.caption: Slide the mirror's side onto the line, and the colours read the same both ways from {7.3|seven point three}: one counting number for each vortex on one side, its long stretch of arrows on the other. Wind the line into the Sacks spiral, and the fold becomes a circle: inside it the first seven counting numbers, outside it the vortices, bands of the spiral that widen toward the rim.

lines.text: Now let the plane climb on, and at every zero keep each eye where it was. The eyes build a tower; vortex one, in cyan, always sits on a circle of radius one.
actions: exp:say:the eyes through the zeros|kept at every zero:  vortex 1 on a circle of radius 1

lines.text: Look straight down the axis. The eyes of ten thousand zeros, stacked: the unit circle of vortex one, and rings for all the others.
actions: exp:say:all 10 000 zeros, down the axis|the vortices belong to the counting numbers
lines.caption: Look straight down the axis. The eyes of {10,000|ten thousand} zeros, stacked: the unit circle of vortex one, and rings for all the others.

lines.text: Look closer: the eyes thin out beyond a faint circle at radius one point seven one, and a brighter ring glows at zero point two nine. At a zero, vortex two's eye is as far from the centre as the path's second vertex: one, plus the arrow of two, one over root two long.
actions: exp:say:a faint circle at r = 1.71|vortex 2's eye:  |1 + 2<sup>−½ − iγ</sup>|,  one plus an arrow 1/√2 long
lines.caption: Look closer: the eyes thin out beyond a faint circle at radius {1.71|one point seven one}, and a brighter ring glows at {0.29|zero point two nine}. At a zero, vortex two's eye is as far from the centre as the path's second vertex: one, plus the arrow of two, {1/√2|one over root two} long.

lines.text: That arrow can point any way, so the eye stays between one minus one over root two and one plus one over root two, and it lingers at those two extremes, so both circles glow. Beyond one point seven one only vortex three and higher can reach, and the eyes thin out.
actions: exp:say:between 1 − 1/√2 = 0.29 and 1 + 1/√2 = 1.71|beyond 1.71 only vortices 3 and up:  the eyes thin out 2.7-fold
lines.caption: That arrow can point any way, so the eye stays between {1 − 1/√2|one minus one over root two} and {1 + 1/√2,|one plus one over root two,} and it lingers at those two extremes, so both circles glow. Beyond {1.71|one point seven one} only vortex three and higher can reach, and the eyes thin out.

lines.text: So the vortices develop as t climbs. New ones are born at the start, the spokes slide outward, and every vortex belongs to a counting number: a reflection of the path's own beginning.
actions: exp:say:how the vortices develop|one per counting number, each a mirror of the path's start

chapters.title: From a zero to E8's heights
chapters.subtitle: the zeros inside E8, part 3:  the turn of n is γ times log n

lines.text: This is E eight's factor funnel. Every counting number sits at its hour on the wheel of thirty, with a column as tall as its logarithm. Seven, at hour seven: one point nine five. Thirty, two times three times five, at hour zero: three point four.
actions: exp:say:E8's factor funnel|n at its hour n mod 30, its column as tall as log n
lines.caption: This is {E8's|E eight's} factor funnel. Every counting number sits at its hour on the wheel of {30|thirty}, with a column as tall as its logarithm. {7,|Seven,} at hour {7|seven}: {log 7 = 1.95.|one point nine five.} {30 = 2 · 3 · 5,|Thirty, two times three times five,} at {hour 0:  log 30 = 3.40.|hour zero: three point four.}

lines.text: Grey it out, and light the powers of two. Two is one piece, log two tall, on the arm of hour two. Four is two pieces, eight is three, sixteen is four: each column is its prime factors' logarithms, stacked.
actions: exp:say:a column is its prime factors, stacked|log 16 = log 2 + log 2 + log 2 + log 2
lines.caption: Grey it out, and light the powers of two. Two is one piece, {log 2|log two} tall, on the arm of hour {2|two}. {4 is 2 pieces, 8 is 3, 16 is 4:|Four is two pieces, eight is three, sixteen is four:} each column is its prime factors' logarithms, stacked.

lines.text: Now the path of partial sums at the first zero, t equal to fourteen point one three, on the funnel's floor. Arrow one, arrow two, arrow three, and on, each one over root n long, each turned by t times log n.
actions: exp:say:the path at the first zero|arrow n:  1/√n long, turned 14.13 · log n
lines.caption: Now the path of partial sums at the first zero, {t =|t equal to} {14.13|fourteen point one three}, on the funnel's floor. Arrow one, arrow two, arrow three, and on, each {1/√n|one over root n} long, each turned by {t · log n.|t times log n.}

lines.text: Its tail closes it on the axis: that is what a zero is. Now lift every arrow to the height of its own number, keeping its direction and its length: arrow two to log two, arrow three to log three, arrow four to log four, twice as high as two. The arrows shrink as they climb, like a horn.
actions: exp:say:lift arrow n to the height log n|keeping its direction −14.13 · log n and its length 1/√n
lines.caption: Its tail closes it on the axis: that is what a zero is. Now lift every arrow to the height of its own number, keeping its direction and its length: arrow two to {log 2|log two}, arrow three to {log 3|log three}, arrow four to {log 4|log four}, twice as high as two. The arrows shrink as they climb, like a horn.

lines.text: Stretch each arrow by the square root of its number, its distance from the centre on the Sacks spiral and on this floor. One over root n times root n is one: every arrow becomes one unit long, and only its direction is left. Through their tips runs a coil that turns by gamma for every unit of height: the zero, wound up E eight's funnel.
actions: exp:say:stretch arrow n by √n|1/√n × √n = 1:  every arrow one unit long, only its direction left
delay:12.98:exp:say:the coil:  the hands at every height|turning 14.13 per unit of height, one turn every 0.44
lines.caption: Stretch each arrow by the square root of its number, its distance from the centre on the Sacks spiral and on this floor. {1/√n × √n = 1:|One over root n times root n is one:} every arrow becomes one unit long, and only its direction is left. Through their tips runs a coil that turns by {γ|gamma} for every unit of height: the zero, wound up {E8's|E eight's} funnel.

lines.text: The coil multiplies by adding heights. Four is two times two, so its hand has turned twice the turn of two. Six is two times three: the turn of two plus the turn of three.
actions: exp:say:multiplying is adding heights|γ·log 4 = 2 γ·log 2   ·   γ·log 6 = γ·log 2 + γ·log 3
lines.caption: The coil multiplies by adding heights. {4 = 2 · 2,|Four is two times two,} so its hand has turned twice the turn of two. {6 = 2 · 3:|Six is two times three:} the turn of two plus the turn of three.

lines.text: Every zero winds its own coil. Twenty-one point zero two turns each hand further, the higher ones more; twenty-five point zero one, further still.
lines.caption: Every zero winds its own coil. {21.02|Twenty-one point zero two} turns each hand further, the higher ones more; {25.01|twenty-five point zero one}, further still.

lines.text: At a height that is not a zero, like eighteen, the hands turn just the same, but drop them back onto the floor and the path does not close: its tail ends away from the axis.
actions: exp:say:t = 18:  not a zero|the arrows dropped back into the path:  it ends away from the axis
lines.caption: At a height that is not a zero, like {18|eighteen}, the hands turn just the same, but drop them back onto the floor and the path does not close: its tail ends away from the axis.

lines.text: That is the bridge between a zero and E eight's layout: the zero's height, times the height of n's column, is the turn of n's arrow. Each prime factor adds its own turn.
actions: exp:say:the bridge|the turn of n at a zero = γ × log n = γ × (the sum of log p over its prime factors)
lines.caption: That is the bridge between a zero and {E8's|E eight's} layout: the zero's height, times the height of n's column, is the turn of n's arrow. Each prime factor adds its own turn.

chapters.title: Lamps and spokes
chapters.subtitle: the zeros inside E8, part 4:  all the coils together

lines.text: Every zero winds its own coil up the funnel. Here are the first three, fourteen point one three, twenty-one point zero two and twenty-five point zero one, over the greyed-out columns.
lines.caption: Every zero winds its own coil up the funnel. Here are the first {three:|three,} {14.13|fourteen point one three}, {21.02|twenty-one point zero two} and {25.01|twenty-five point zero one}, over the greyed-out columns.

lines.text: Take all ten thousand five hundred zeros, and look at one height: the top of seven's column. Each coil points somewhere there; on average they lean towards minus one, by minus point one one five, exactly as Landau's formula predicts for a prime.
actions: exp:say:at the height of 7, a prime|10 500 coils lean to −1:  mean −0.115,  Landau −0.115
lines.caption: Take all {10,500|ten thousand five hundred} zeros, and look at one height: the top of seven's column. Each coil points somewhere there; on average they lean towards {−1|minus one}, by {−0.115|minus point one one five}, exactly as Landau's formula predicts for a prime.

lines.text: At the top of six's column, two times three, the coils point every way, and their mean is zero. The zeros lean only at the powers of primes.
actions: exp:say:at the height of 6 = 2·3|the coils cancel:  mean 0.000
lines.caption: At the top of six's column, {6 = 2 · 3,|two times three,} the coils point every way, and their mean is zero. The zeros lean only at the powers of primes.

lines.text: Now do it at every height. A ring climbs the axis, and at each height all the coils add up to one hand, drawn out to the side. Where they agree, at a prime power, it shoots out to the top of that prime's column: seven, eight, nine. At six, ten and twelve it stays at the axis.
actions: exp:say:all the coils, height by height|a tooth of log p at every prime power
lines.caption: Now do it at every height. A ring climbs the axis, and at each height all the coils add up to one hand, drawn out to the side. Where they agree, at a prime power, it shoots out to the top of that prime's column: {7, 8, 9.|seven, eight, nine.} At {6|six}, {10|ten} and {12|twelve} it stays at the axis.

lines.text: Climbing on, it lights every prime power up to four hundred: a comb, the master wave from the first discovery, stood up along the logarithm.
actions: exp:say:ζ's comb|a tooth at every prime power
lines.caption: Climbing on, it lights every prime power up to {400|four hundred}: a comb, the master wave from the first discovery, stood up along the logarithm.

lines.text: But the comb is the same in every direction. Spin it round the axis, slowly, and watch each tooth sweep out a ring through its prime's column. Zeta's zeros know how high a prime sits, not its hour on the wheel.
actions: exp:say:spun round the axis:  a ring per prime power|ζ's zeros fix the height, not the hour

lines.text: E eight knows more. Its field has eight L-functions, and at the height of seven each one's zeros light the tooth of seven, turned by its own character: along one, minus one, i or minus i.
actions: exp:say:eight L-functions at the height of 7|each tooth turned by its character χ(7):  1, −1, i or −i
lines.caption: {E8|E eight} knows more. Its field has eight L-functions, and at the height of seven each one's zeros light the tooth of seven, turned by its own character: along {1, −1, i or −i.|one, minus one, i or minus i.}

lines.text: Turn each one back by its character at an hour, and chain the eight. At every other hour they cancel; only at hour seven do all eight line up, and the chain swings onto the spoke of seven.
actions: exp:say:turned back by χ(h), and chained|the eight line up only for the hour of 7
lines.caption: Turn each one back by its character at an hour, and chain the eight. At every other hour they cancel; only at hour {7|seven} do all eight line up, and the chain swings onto {the spoke of 7.|the spoke of seven.}

lines.text: Do this at every height, and the comb splits into eight fans, one for each gold hour: only the primes on spoke h survive in fan h.
actions: exp:say:eight L-functions, eight fans|only the primes on spoke h survive

chapters.title: 240 roots, infinitely many numbers
chapters.subtitle: the zeros inside E8, part 5:  E8's clock and E8's shells

lines.text: E eight has two hundred and forty roots, shown here in its Coxeter plane as eight rings of thirty. So how can so few points hold infinitely many counting numbers?
actions: exp:say:E8:  240 roots|8 rings of 30 in the Coxeter plane
lines.caption: {E8|E eight} has {240|two hundred and forty} roots, shown here in its Coxeter plane as eight rings of {30|thirty}. So how can so few points hold infinitely many counting numbers?

lines.text: They don't have to. The roots set E eight's clock: its Coxeter element turns the plane by a thirtieth of a turn, so the wheel has thirty hours, and eight of them, E eight's exponents, are gold.
lines.caption: They don't have to. The roots set {E8's|E eight's} clock: its Coxeter element turns the plane by a thirtieth of a turn, so the wheel has {30|thirty} hours, and eight of them, {E8's|E eight's} exponents, are gold.

lines.text: Drop every counting number onto the wheel at its hour, n mod thirty, one turn further out each time round. The spiral never ends.
actions: exp:say:every n at its hour|n mod 30:  the hours repeat, the radius grows
lines.caption: Drop every counting number onto the wheel at its hour, {n mod 30,|n mod thirty,} one turn further out each time round. The spiral never ends.

lines.text: Grey it out and follow one hour, its arm drawn from the centre. Seven, thirty-seven, sixty-seven and ninety-seven all land on hour seven, each one turn further out: all four are primes. One hundred and twenty-seven, too.
lines.caption: Grey it out and follow one hour, its arm drawn from the centre. {7|Seven}, {37|thirty-seven}, {67|sixty-seven} and {97|ninety-seven} all land on hour {7|seven}, each one turn further out: all four are primes. {127|One hundred and twenty-seven}, too.

lines.text: Hour six holds six, thirty-six, sixty-six and ninety-six: every one a multiple of six, off the gold spokes. The clock sorts out two, three and five; the rest it cannot see.
actions: exp:say:hour 6:  6, 36, 66, 96|multiples of 6, off the gold spokes
lines.caption: Hour {6|six} holds {6|six}, {36|thirty-six}, {66|sixty-six} and {96|ninety-six}: every one a multiple of six, off the gold spokes. The clock sorts out two, three and five; the rest it cannot see.

lines.text: And E eight itself is not two hundred and forty points. It is an infinite lattice, and the roots are only its first shell: the points at distance root two. Tilt the wheel, and the next shells appear beneath it.
actions: exp:say:E8 is a lattice:  shells|the 240 roots are its first shell, at distance √2
lines.caption: And {E8|E eight} itself is not {240|two hundred and forty} points. It is an infinite lattice, and the roots are only its first shell: the points at distance {√2.|root two.} Tilt the wheel, and the next shells appear beneath it.

lines.text: Each shell n holds the points at distance root two n: two thousand one hundred and sixty for n equal to two, six thousand seven hundred and twenty for three, seventeen thousand five hundred and twenty for four, and on down to seven. Every counting number has a shell of its own.
actions: exp:say:a shell for every counting number|shell n:  the points at distance √2n:  240, 2 160, 6 720, 17 520, …
lines.caption: Each shell n holds the points at distance {√(2n):|root two n:} {2,160|two thousand one hundred and sixty} for {n =|n equal to} {2|two}, {6,720|six thousand seven hundred and twenty} {for 3,|for three,} {17,520|seventeen thousand five hundred and twenty} {for 4,|for four,} and on down to {7.|seven.} Every counting number has a shell of its own.

lines.text: Each shell's size is two hundred and forty times a sum of cubes, one cube for each divisor of n. One has the single cube one. Two has one and eight. Three has one and twenty-seven.
actions: exp:say:shell n holds 240 σ<sub>3</sub>(n) points|σ<sub>3</sub>(n):  one cube d³ for each divisor d of n
lines.caption: Each shell's size is {240|two hundred and forty} times a sum of cubes, one cube for each divisor of n. {1 has the single cube 1.|One has the single cube one.} {2 has 1 and 8.|Two has one and eight.} {3 has 1 and 27.|Three has one and twenty-seven.}

lines.text: Four has one, eight and sixty-four: its divisors one, two and four. Five, a prime, has only one and a hundred and twenty-five. Six has four cubes: one, eight, twenty-seven and two hundred and sixteen. Seven, a prime, has one and three hundred and forty-three.
lines.caption: {4 has 1, 8 and 64:|Four has one, eight and sixty-four:} its divisors {1, 2 and 4.|one, two and four.} {5,|Five,} a prime, has only {1|one} and {125|a hundred and twenty-five}. {6|Six} has four cubes: {1|one}, {8|eight}, {27|twenty-seven} and {216|two hundred and sixteen}. {7,|Seven,} a prime, has {1|one} and {343|three hundred and forty-three}.

lines.text: So the shells are linked by divisibility: each shell sends its cube to the shells of its multiples. One feeds every shell. Two feeds four and six. Three feeds six.
actions: exp:say:linked by divisibility|shell d sends d³ to every shell n that d divides
lines.caption: So the shells are linked by divisibility: each shell sends its cube to the shells of its multiples. {1|One} feeds every shell. {2 feeds 4 and 6.|Two feeds four and six.} {3 feeds 6.|Three feeds six.}

lines.text: That is why the shells are a useful way to look at numbers. A prime's shell holds the fewest points it can, just one and p cubed. Every extra cube is a divisor: six's extra cubes, eight and twenty-seven, are two cubed and three cubed, so E eight's geometry has factored six.

A prime's shell holds the fewest points it can, just {1 and p³.|one and p cubed.} Every extra cube is a divisor: {6's|six's} extra cubes, {8|eight} and {27|twenty-seven}, are {2³ and 3³,|two cubed and three cubed,} so {E8's|E eight's} geometry has factored {6.|six.}

lines.text: Counted over every shell at once, the points of E eight give its own zeta function: two hundred and forty times zeta of s, times zeta of s minus three. A finite symmetry, and infinitely many shells, one for every counting number.
actions: exp:unmute:E8 tower A,E8 tower B/floor 4,E8 cubes 1,E8 cubes 2,E8 cubes 3,E8 cubes 4,E8 links:2
exp:say:Σ 240 σ<sub>3</sub>(n) n<sup>−s</sup> = 240 ζ(s) ζ(s − 3)|a finite symmetry, a shell for every counting number
lines.caption: Counted over every shell at once, the points of {E8|E eight} give its own zeta function: {240 ζ(s) ζ(s − 3).|two hundred and forty times zeta of s, times zeta of s minus three.} A finite symmetry, and infinitely many shells, one for every counting number.

chapters.title: The twist on the twist
chapters.subtitle: squares that orbit the links of zeta's chain

lines.text: Claude, an AI math research assistant, and I gave every link of zeta's chain a square. This is the chain at the three hundredth zero, t equal to five hundred forty-one point eight five: a link for every counting number.
actions: exp:say:the twist on the twist|a square on every link of zeta's chain
delay:5.49:exp:say:zeta's chain at zero 300|t = 541.85:  link n is n<sup>−½</sup> long, turned t · log n
lines.caption: Claude, an AI math research assistant, and I gave every link of zeta's chain a square. This is the chain at the {300th|three hundredth} zero, {t =|t equal to} {541.85|five hundred forty-one point eight five}: a link for every counting number.

lines.text: Link n is one over root n long. Stand a fin of the same length at its start, perpendicular to it, and the link and its fin are two sides of a square, of area one over n.
actions: exp:say:a square on every link|link n and its fin:  a square of area 1/n
lines.caption: Link n is {1/√n|one over root n} long. Stand a fin of the same length at its start, perpendicular to it, and the link and its fin are two sides of a square, of area {1/n.|one over n.}

lines.text: Now the twist on the twist. While each link turns clockwise by t times log n, let each fin turn about its own link by alpha times log n, so that it orbits its joint: gold where it points up out of the plane, cyan where it points down.
actions: exp:say:the twist on the twist|each fin turns α · log n:  gold up, cyan down
lines.caption: Now the twist on the twist. While each link turns clockwise by {t · log n,|t times log n,} let each fin turn about its own link by {α · log n,|alpha times log n,} so that it orbits its joint: gold where it points up out of the plane, cyan where it points down.

lines.text: Stop at alpha equal to t over two, half the chain's rate. In spoke k, where each link turns k whole turns from the last, its fin turns k half-turns. So in the odd spokes the fins flip from link to link, and in the even spokes they line up.
actions: exp:say:α = t/2|in spoke k a link turns its fin k half-turns
lines.caption: Stop at {α = t/2,|alpha equal to t over two,} half the chain's rate. In spoke k, where each link turns k whole turns from the last, its fin turns k half-turns. So in the odd spokes the fins flip from link to link, and in the even spokes they line up.

lines.text: At alpha equal to t, the chain's own rate, each fin tilts by its own link's angle, so the fins line up wherever the links do.
actions: exp:say:α = t:  the chain's own rate|each fin tilts by its own link's angle
lines.caption: At {α = t,|alpha equal to t,} the chain's own rate, each fin tilts by its own link's angle, so the fins line up wherever the links do.

lines.text: Now add the fins up, head to tail, seen from above. Half of every fin points the same way, straight up the plane, so the sum runs off along a straight road: the chain at height zero, which never turns.
actions: exp:say:the fins, head to tail|half of each fin points up:  a road, Σ 1/(2√n)

lines.text: Take the road away, and what is left is half the chain an octave up, at two t. So the twist on the twist is a beat: the fins carry two zeta chains, at t minus alpha and t plus alpha.
actions: exp:say:the road taken away|left:  half the chain at 2t, an octave up
delay:6.58:exp:say:a beat|the fins in the plane:  (i/2)(S(t − α) + S(t + α))
lines.caption: Take the road away, and what is left is half the chain an octave up, at {2t.|two t.} So the twist on the twist is a beat: the fins carry two zeta chains, at {t − α|t minus alpha} and {t + α.|t plus alpha.}

lines.text: This octave chain runs straight where the chain itself runs straight, in its spoke near n equal to eighty-six. And it runs straight through the chain's knot near one hundred seventy-two, where the chain curls up tight. The twist on the twist turns knots into spokes.
actions: exp:say:knots become spokes|the octave runs straight at spokes and knots
lines.caption: This octave chain runs straight where the chain itself runs straight, in its spoke near {n =|n equal to} {86|eighty-six}. And it runs straight through the chain's knot near {172|one hundred seventy-two}, where the chain curls up tight. The twist on the twist turns knots into spokes.

lines.text: Now the Sacks spiral, where every number n sits at radius root n. The radius is the square root itself, so a radius and a fin as long make a square of area n.
actions: exp:say:the Sacks spiral|n at radius √n:  radius and fin, a square of area n
lines.caption: Now the Sacks spiral, where every number n sits at radius {√n.|root n.} The radius is the square root itself, so a radius and a fin as long make a square of area n.

lines.text: Give every number its fin, drawn at a quarter of its length, and turn each fin about its radius by the first zero's phase, gamma times log n. The fins point down in rings, on the zero's crests, and up between them.
actions: exp:say:each fin turned by the first zero|φ = γ<sub>1</sub> log n − τ/4:  the fin's height −√n cos(γ<sub>1</sub> log n)
lines.caption: Give every number its fin, drawn at a quarter of its length, and turn each fin about its radius by the first zero's phase, {γ · log n.|gamma times log n.} The fins point down in rings, on the zero's crests, and up between them.

lines.text: Now add the fins turned by the second zero, the third, and on up to ten thousand zeros, each sum divided by T over tau. The fins shrink away, except on the prime powers, where they stand up straight.
actions: exp:say:summed over the zeros|K zeros' fins added, ÷ T/τ  (T: the K-th zero)
lines.caption: Now add the fins turned by the second zero, the third, and on up to {10,000|ten thousand} zeros, each sum divided by {T/τ.|T over tau.} The fins shrink away, except on the prime powers, where they stand up straight.

lines.text: Landau proved why. Added up to height T, the zeros' waves give minus T over tau, times log p over root n, at every power n of a prime p. The fin's length, root n, cancels the one over root n, so each needle stands at log p.
actions: exp:say:Landau|Σ<sub>γ ≤ T</sub> n<sup>iγ</sup> = −(T/τ) Λ(n)/√n + O(log T)
lines.caption: Landau proved why. Added up to height T, the zeros' waves give {−(T/τ) · log p/√n|minus T over tau, times log p over root n,} at every power n of a prime p. The fin's length, {√n,|root n,} cancels the {1/√n|one over root n}, so each needle stands at log p.

lines.text: Three hundred seventy-nine is a prime: its needle reaches five point seven eight, nearly log three seventy-nine. Three hundred sixty-one, nineteen squared, reaches two point eight, nearly log nineteen. And three hundred seventy-one, seven times fifty-three, stays at zero.

And {371|three hundred seventy-one}, {7 · 53,|seven times fifty-three,} stays at zero.

lines.text: So the twist on the twist creates nothing new: it rearranges the chain's vortices into a beat of two chains. And on the Sacks spiral, the side of each number's square is exactly the weight that stands the zeros' waves up on the primes.
actions: exp:say:what the twist shows|two chains in a beat;  √n is Landau's weight
